traveler: Khwaja Mu'in al-Din Hasan Chishti (Moinuddin Chishti), Gharib Nawaz
title: The Mill and the Dargah: from Sistan to Ajmer, and the Order that Walked to India
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Sanjar, the birth in Sistan
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The first of February is the tradition's day. Most modern encyclopedic sources give 1143 (536 AH) after Currie; some hagiographic chronologies give 530 AH, 1136. No contemporary record fixes either. Coordinates are approximate, keyed to the modern Sistan district around Zabol.
stops.campa: In the village of Sanjar, in the Sistan of the eastern Iranian plateau, a son is born to Khwaja Ghiyath al-Din Hasan and Umm al-Wara, whom the tradition also calls Bibi Mahe Noor. The house owns a grinding mill and an orchard, enough to make the family known in its district and not enough to make it rich. They name the boy Mu'in al-Din. No chronicle of the thirteenth century records the day. The date comes down through the order he will found, which counts it the first of February and cannot agree with itself whether the year is 1143 or 1136.
suggested_refs: The Sistan basin around Zabol, on the modern Iran-Afghanistan border
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mu'in al-Din Chishti', citing P. M. Currie, The Shrine and Cult of Mu'in al-Din Chishti of Ajmer (1989)

stops.name: Sistan, the dervish at the orchard gate
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Hagiographic chronologies place the encounter at about age nine, c. 1150-1151. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: A wandering mystic named Ibrahim Qandozi comes through the orchard where the boy is working. Moinuddin, nine years old by the count the order keeps, brings him fruit, and the dervish gives him a piece of bread. He eats it. What the tradition says happens next is that the orchard, the mill and the inheritance all go thin at once, and the boy begins to want something the district cannot supply. The story is a conversion topos told of many saints in many countries. It is also the only account of his childhood that anyone has.
suggested_refs: The bread of Ibrahim Qandozi, the conversion topos of the Chishti hagiographies

stops.name: Sistan, the mill sold and the road taken
stops.date_confidence: contested. Wikipedia gives the father's death c. 1155; the devotional chronologies give 544 AH, 1150. The sources agree on the mill and the orchard and disagree on the year by five.
stops.campa: Ghiyath al-Din dies, and the mill and the orchard pass to a son of fifteen or sixteen who does not want them. He sells them, or gives them away, and hands the proceeds to the poor of the district. Then he walks out of Sistan with nothing, which is the condition the Sufi manuals require and which very few of the men who write about it have actually met. He is not yet anybody's disciple. He has no teacher, no order, no destination, and no property, and the last of those is the only one he has chosen.
suggested_refs: The grinding mill and orchard of the Hasan family, sold to fund a life of wandering study

stops.name: Khorasan, the road out of Sistan
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Devotional sources place a family migration in the 1150s without a year; the Oghuz revolt that fixes the context is 1153. Month arbitrary. The pin is Nishapur, used as a proxy for Khorasan, and the atlas already carries this coordinate.
stops.campa: The Seljuk order that has held the eastern plateau for a century is breaking. Oghuz Turkmen have risen against Sultan Ahmad Sanjar, taken him captive in 1153, and left Khorasan open to whoever can hold a road. Families move north out of Sistan toward the cities where scholarship and money still concentrate, and Moinuddin moves with them, a boy with no property walking into the country of Nishapur. Attar is a child in Nishapur, ten or eleven years old. Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri has been dead eighty years, and the Sufi curriculum he fixed in prose is what the seminaries ahead will teach.
suggested_refs: The Oghuz revolt of 1153 and the capture of Sultan Ahmad Sanjar
sources: corrected against the standard chronology of Ahmad Sanjar's defeat by Oghuz Turkmen, 1153

stops.name: Bukhara, the seminary quarter
stops.date_confidence: undated in every source. Wikipedia names Bukhara and Samarkand as his schooling and gives no years; devotional chronologies imply c. 1150-1160. Placed here for route order only.
stops.campa: He enrolls in a Bukhara madrasa and takes the ordinary course: grammar, Qur'anic science, hadith, jurisprudence. Bukhara has manufactured Sunni legal scholars for two hundred years and will manufacture them for sixty more, until the Mongols burn it. Popular tradition names his teachers Maulana Husamuddin and Maulana Sharfuddin, names that appear in devotional chronologies and in no academic source anyone has checked them against. What the schooling gives him is the equipment to argue in front of a court. The wandering years will consume all of it.
suggested_refs: The madrasas of Bukhara before the Mongol sack of 1220
sources: haqqfinder.com chronology for the teachers' names, unverified

stops.name: Samarkand, the seminary quarter
stops.date_confidence: undated. Same source position as Bukhara. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: From Bukhara he crosses to Samarkand, the other pole of the same learning, and continues in the sciences of the Book. The city holds the tomb of Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, the theologian whose school supplies the doctrinal frame the Chishti order will carry into India, and the students go out to it. Moinuddin goes. He is finishing an education that qualifies him to hold a chair, sit as a judge, or teach law for a salary, and the record of his life contains no day on which he does any of the three.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Abu Mansur al-Maturidi at Samarkand, 39.658, 66.975

stops.name: Hartang, the tomb of Imam al-Bukhari
stops.date_confidence: traditional and undated. Coordinate corrected: the incoming pool gave 39.5766, 66.6835, open country southwest of Samarkand, an error of about 35 km. The Memorial Complex of Imam al-Bukhari stands at Hartang, roughly 25 km north of the city.
stops.campa: Twenty-five kilometres north of Samarkand, at the village of Hartang, lies Muhammad al-Bukhari, who sifted six hundred thousand reports of the Prophet down to some seven thousand and gave Sunni Islam the second book on its shelf. The student comes out from the city to stand at the grave. He is at the end of the formal training and the beginning of the other thing: a jurist's pilgrimage made in the manner the Sufis make pilgrimages, to a dead man rather than to a living chair.
suggested_refs: The Memorial Complex of Imam al-Bukhari at Hartang, Samarkand province
sources: coordinate from the Memorial Complex of Imam al-Bukhari, 39 deg 48 min 54 sec N, 66 deg 56 min 40 sec E

segments.name: The Master and the City of Peace

stops.name: Nishapur, the meeting with Usman Harooni
stops.date_confidence: traditional, undated in all sources. Some tellings place the first meeting in a village called Haroon rather than in the city. Year assigned for route order only.
stops.campa: In the district of Nishapur he meets Khwaja Usman Harooni and does not leave him again. The tradition calls the discipleship twenty years and elsewhere calls it two and a half, and the sources that give both numbers give no dates at all. What the meeting ends is the school. Moinuddin holds credentials and Harooni holds none that any madrasa recognizes, and the younger man puts himself under the older one for a term nobody records the length of. This is Attar's city, and Qushayri's, and the city Baha ud-Din Walad's household will abandon in flight.
suggested_refs: Khwaja Usman Harooni, Chishti shaykh of the Nishapur district

stops.name: Haroon, the years in the master's company
stops.date_confidence: undated, and the coordinate is an admission of ignorance. The village of Haroon implied by Harooni's nisba is not located in any reachable source; the pin is Nishapur's, offset, and stands as a placeholder rather than a finding. Sources disagree sharply on the length of the discipleship, from over twenty years to two and a half.
stops.campa: The apprenticeship is itinerant. Master and disciple move on a circuit of villages and shrine towns, and what passes between them is not a syllabus but a manner of living: the fast, the night watch, the poverty that is chosen rather than suffered, the refusal of gifts from anyone who governs. Harooni's own nisba points to a village called Haroon, which no reachable source locates, so this pin sits beside Nishapur and admits as much. Twenty years of a man's life are stored in one coordinate, and the coordinate is a guess.
suggested_refs: The unlocated village of Haroon, named only by Usman Harooni's nisba

stops.name: Baghdad, Bab al-Azaj and the shaykh Abd al-Qadir
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Wikipedia mentions the meeting and gives no date; one popular chronology dates it 551 AH, 1156. Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani dies in 1166, so any meeting must precede that. Canonical Bab al-Azaj pin inherited from abd_al_qadir_al_jilani.journey.json.
stops.campa: The circuit reaches Baghdad. At Bab al-Azaj, the eastern quarter where Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani has taught for thirty years and where he will die within the year, Chishti tradition brings the two men face to face and has the old Hanbali prophesy the young Persian's greatness. Jilani's own file in this atlas flags his lineage claims as contested, and the Chishti visit is not in it. This is a later order writing itself a receipt from an earlier one, and the receipt is dated a year before the signatory dies.
suggested_refs: The school of Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani at Bab al-Azaj, Baghdad

stops.name: Baghdad, the tomb of Junayd
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Chishti biography places him at Junayd's grave during the Baghdad years without a date. Canonical pin inherited from junayd_al_baghdadi.journey.json.
stops.campa: A short way west, in the Shunizi ground, Junayd al-Baghdadi lies beside his uncle Sari al-Saqati. The Chishti chain of transmission runs back through this grave: the sober school, which keeps the law and the ecstasy in the same hand and dies in bed. Ibn Arabi will pray here in 1205, and the household of Baha ud-Din Walad will pass through in 1219 on its way out of a burning Khorasan. Moinuddin comes first, or the tradition says he does, and takes from the stone the ancestry his order will claim.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Junayd and Sari al-Saqati in the Shunizi cemetery, Baghdad

stops.name: Baghdad, the execution ground of al-Hallaj
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The station is fixed and canonical in the atlas; Chishti's presence at it is inference from the route his hagiography gives him, not a source claim.
stops.campa: On the west bank stands the place where al-Hallaj was flogged, mutilated and burned in 922 for saying in public what the sober school says only in private. Every Sufi who comes through Baghdad walks past it. Attar will stand here in 1179 and write the death down, and the students of Jilani's generation cross the square on their errands without stopping. It is the boundary marker of the trade Moinuddin has entered: the exact distance between the ecstasy and the scaffold, measured out in one square of ground.
suggested_refs: The execution ground of al-Hallaj, 26 March 922, west bank of Baghdad

stops.name: Isfahan, the Friday Mosque
stops.date_confidence: undated devotional route-list entry, c.1160s-1180s. Coordinate corrected: the pool labelled the stop the Jameh Mosque quarter but pinned 32.6572, 51.6776, the bazaar area 1.6 km southwest. Pin moved onto the mosque.
stops.campa: The road bends back onto the Iranian plateau. At Isfahan the Friday Mosque has been rebuilt by the Seljuks into the largest congregational space in Persia, two brick domes and a forest of piers, and the city is thick with jurists. He passes through it as a name on a list: the devotional itineraries record the stop and record nothing that happens there. The list is long, the years are undated, and this is what most of the middle of his life amounts to in the record, a sequence of great cities and no events.
suggested_refs: The Jameh Mosque of Isfahan, Seljuk rebuilding

stops.name: Tabriz, the city of the scholars
stops.date_confidence: undated devotional route-list entry, c.1160s-1180s. Year assigned for route order only.
stops.campa: Tabriz, at the northwestern corner of the circuit, is the last large Muslim city before the Caucasus and a station on every eastward road. The itineraries put him here between Astarabad and the return leg and say nothing else. Two hundred miles north, Nizami of Ganja, born in the same year the tradition gives Moinuddin, is at work on the romances that will settle the shape of Persian narrative verse. The two men never meet and never mention each other, and the atlas holds them in one decade on one plateau.
suggested_refs: Tabriz as a station on the Khorasan-to-Anatolia road in the twelfth century

stops.name: Kharaqan, the tomb of Abu'l-Hasan
stops.date_confidence: undated. Coordinate corrected: the pool gave 36.3, 55.0, a suspiciously round guess landing in empty desert. The Tomb of Abu al-Hassan Kharaqani stands at Qaleh Now-e Kharaqan, about 24 km north of Shahrud in Semnan province, an error of roughly 37 km.
stops.campa: North of Shahrud, in a village of the Semnan country, lies Abu'l-Hasan Kharaqani, the unlettered farmer whom Bayazid's spirit is said to have summoned across a hundred years and who told visitors that the Sufi is the one with nothing left to want. Moinuddin turns aside for the grave. The route he is following is not a route between cities. It is a route between dead men, and the living stops on it exist only because the dead ones are lying there.
suggested_refs: The Tomb of Abu al-Hassan Kharaqani, Qaleh Now-e Kharaqan, Semnan province
sources: coordinate from the Tomb of Abu al-Hassan Kharaqani, 36 deg 38 min 02 sec N, 55 deg 04 min 09 sec E

stops.name: Merv, the oasis of the copyists
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, twice over. The stop is rendered Memna in the source, a toponym corresponding to nothing known; identification with Merv is this file's best guess and not a source claim. The date is assigned for route order.
stops.campa: Merv holds ten libraries and the largest gathering of manuscripts in the eastern Islamic world, and the Seljuk sultan whose fall emptied Khorasan lies under its blue dome. One devotional source names a stop it calls Memna, a name matching no known place, and Merv is the nearest thing on the road. Within forty years the Mongols will kill the city so completely that the libraries, the copyists and the name all go together, and nothing of what he sees here outlives him.
suggested_refs: The libraries of Merv and the tomb of Sultan Ahmad Sanjar, destroyed 1221
sources: identification with Merv flagged as reconstruction

stops.name: Herat, the Friday Mosque and the road to Chisht
stops.date_confidence: undated devotional route-list entry. Year assigned for route order only.
stops.campa: At Herat the Masjid-i Jami stands on the eastern approach to the Iranian world, and ninety miles up the Hari Rud valley sits the town of Chisht, where Abu Ishaq Shami taught two and a half centuries earlier and from which the order takes its name. Moinuddin will carry that name across a subcontinent that has never heard it. He does not found the Chishtiyya. He is the man who moves it, and the move starts on this road, which from here runs east and stops running west.
suggested_refs: The Friday Mosque of Herat; the town of Chisht in the Hari Rud valley

stops.name: Baghdad, the parting from Usman Harooni
stops.date_confidence: traditional and undated; the tradition fixes it by his age, fifty-two, which against a 1143 birth gives 1195 and against 1136 gives 1188. The year here is a route-order placeholder and the arithmetic does not close.
stops.campa: At fifty-two, by the tradition's count, he parts from his master in Baghdad. Harooni names him successor, seats him on the prayer mat, and hands over relics the order holds to have belonged to the Prophet. The apprenticeship is over and there is no institution waiting to receive him: no chair, no endowment, no congregation, no city that has asked for him. What he owns is a mat, a bundle of relics, and the authority of one dead lineage to speak in its own name.
suggested_refs: The relics of the Prophet transmitted in the Chishti succession

stops.name: Mecca, the Kaaba
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Devotional chronology dates the Hajj to 583 AH, 1187, with Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki as companion; other sources place it simply after he receives the khirqa. Canonical Kaaba pin, inherited byte-identical from the atlas.
stops.campa: He makes the Hajj, with Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki beside him in the accounts that name a companion. The Kaaba is the fixed point of this whole atlas: Nizami's father circles it in 1189, the household of Baha ud-Din Walad in the spring of 1220, and Ibn Arabi receives at this stone in 1202 the vision of the Youth that opens the Meccan Revelations. Moinuddin arrives fifteen years before Ibn Arabi and walks the same circuit, an unknown Khorasani with a mat and no country.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Grand Mosque of Mecca, canonical pin of the Sufi cluster

stops.name: Medina, the Prophet's Mosque and the command
stops.date_confidence: traditional, undated. Wikipedia references a dream leading him to India without fixing a date; the vision at Medina is a staple of the hagiographic corpus, not a documented event. Month arbitrary.
stops.campa: At Medina he keeps the vigil beside the tomb, and the tradition places here the instruction that decides everything after it: go to Ajmer in Hindustan and be my representative there. Nothing about the vision is documented. Ajmer is two thousand miles east, in a country under a Hindu king, where no Chishti has ever set foot and where the language is none of the three he speaks. He turns around and starts walking, and every stop from here on is on that errand.
stops.quote: It is told that once when he went to perform the pilgrimage to the holy tomb of the Prophet Muhammad, one day from the inside of the pure and blessed tomb a cry came: Send for Muinuddin.
stops.quote_source: Allah Diya Chishti, Siyar al-Aqtab (1647), translated and quoted on Wikiquote citing Currie
suggested_refs: The Prophet's Mosque at Medina and the Rawda

stops.name: Balkh, Maulana Ziauddin taken as disciple
stops.date_confidence: traditional. Sufiwiki's chronology attaches a Balkh stop and the recruitment of Maulana Ziauddin to 1200 CE, on a leg it also describes as travel away from an Ajmer he has supposedly settled in permanently since 1192. The date here is placed on the outward road instead; the inconsistency is the source's.
stops.campa: On the eastward road he stops at Balkh, under the ruined stucco of the No Gunbad mosque, and takes Maulana Ziauddin as a disciple, one of the few individual recruitments the middle years record by name. Balkh is Ibrahim ibn Adham's city, the prince who walked out of a throne into the desert five centuries before, and it is the city the family of Baha ud-Din Walad will abandon in 1219 with the Mongols a season behind them. Moinuddin passes through it while it is still standing.
suggested_refs: The No Gunbad mosque at Balkh, the oldest surviving Islamic building in Afghanistan

stops.name: Multan, the tenth of Muharram
stops.date_confidence: badly contested. One chronology dates the Multan arrival to 10 Muharram 561 AH, 1165 CE, which is twenty-two years before the same tradition's Hajj and twenty-six before its Ajmer settlement; Wikipedia places the South Asian arrival in the early thirteenth century. The year here is a route-order placeholder between two irreconcilable calendars.
stops.campa: He crosses into the Indus country and reaches Multan on the tenth of Muharram, the day of Ashura, in the company of his cousin Khwaja Syed Fakhr al-Din Gardezi Chishti. Multan is where al-Hallaj is said to have gone two and a half centuries before him on the same eastward reach, and it is the first Muslim city of the subcontinent, a frontier town of shrines and canals. From here the road runs up to Lahore and then southeast into a country the Ghurid armies are in the middle of taking.
suggested_refs: Multan, the westernmost Muslim city of the Indus plain in the twelfth century

stops.name: Lahore, the tomb of Ali Hujwiri
stops.date_confidence: the event is attested, the date is not. Wikipedia records the Lahore meditation and attaches no year, placing his South Asian arrival in the early thirteenth century. The pool carried this as attested with the date 1192; that anchor is withdrawn here and the year is a placeholder.
stops.campa: At Lahore he goes first to the grave of Ali Hujwiri, called Data Ganj Bakhsh, who came east from Ghazna more than a century before him and wrote the Kashf al-Mahjub, the first treatise on Sufism composed in Persian. He sits at the tomb and meditates before continuing. It is the correct order of operations for what he is about to attempt: the Persian Sufism of Khorasan has already been carried into the Punjab once, by a man buried here, and Moinuddin takes the road onward from that stone.
suggested_refs: Data Darbar, the shrine of Ali Hujwiri at Lahore

stops.name: Ajmer, the camp above Ana Sagar
stops.date_confidence: devotional tradition only. Popular chronology gives the first Ajmer arrival with forty followers as 587 AH, 1191; Wikipedia gives no Ana Sagar episode and places the South Asian arrival in the early thirteenth century. The pool tagged this attested; it is reconstruction. Coordinate moved onto the lake, which centres about 1.6 km west of the pool's pin.
stops.campa: He comes into Ajmer with forty men and camps on the hill above Ana Sagar lake, in sight of the temples along its shore and of the Chahamana capital below. The town is Prithviraj Chauhan's, the ground is not Muslim ground, and the party has no permission to be on it. The hill will be walled and named Chillah Khwaja Sahib and folded into the shrine's devotional geography. On the day itself it is forty strangers, a lake, and a camp nobody has authorised.
stops.quote: If God and His Prophet so will, it will not be long before I raze to the ground these idol temples.
stops.quote_source: Allah Diya Chishti, Siyar al-Aqtab (1647), trans. in P. M. Currie, The Shrine and Cult of Mu'in al-Din Chishti of Ajmer (OUP, 1989); attributed to him on seeing the temples around Ana Sagar, four centuries after his death
suggested_refs: Chillah Khwaja Sahib on the hill above Ana Sagar lake, Ajmer

stops.name: Ajmer, the khanqah under the hill
stops.date_confidence: two irreconcilable traditions. The devotional canon dates the settlement to 1192 and folds it into Muhammad of Ghor's victory over Prithviraj at Tarain; Wikipedia, the attested source, places his arrival in the early thirteenth century and his Delhi visit during Iltutmish's reign, which begins 1211. The pool tagged 1192 as attested; that tag is withdrawn. Coordinate of the Dargah is correct.
stops.campa: He settles below the hill and builds a hospice: a room to teach in, a floor for travellers, a kitchen. The Chishti rule he plants there takes no money from rulers, admits anyone through the door, and feeds whoever comes. The devotional canon dates the settlement to the year Muhammad of Ghor breaks Prithviraj at Tarain, and welds the two events into one. The modern reading puts him in Ajmer under Iltutmish, twenty years later, arriving to a town already taken. The dargah stands on this ground.
stops.quote: You are not truly of my religion if you depart in any way from my sunnat.
stops.quote_source: Allah Diya Chishti, Siyar al-Aqtab (1647), trans. in Currie; framed as the Prophet's words to Mu'in al-Din in a visionary episode, not as his own
suggested_refs: The site of the khanqah at Ajmer, later the Dargah Sharif

stops.name: Ajmer, the contest with the ascetics
stops.date_confidence: undated hagiography. No independent chronicle of the period corroborates any specific episode; the causal link between his arrival and the Ghurid conquest is a later elaboration, not a contemporary record.
stops.campa: The hagiography of the Ajmer years is a war of miracles: yogis who fly and are brought down, court magicians outmatched, temple attendants converted, a lake drunk into a bowl. No contemporary chronicle records any of it. What the cycle encodes is the fact underneath, that a Persian Sufi with forty men walked into a Rajput capital and stayed, and that the older religious establishment did not remove him. Later chroniclers go further and credit him with the conquest itself.
stops.quote: We have caught Rai Pithaura alive and have given him to the army of Islam.
stops.quote_source: Amir Khwurd, Siyaru'l-Auliya (14th c.), trans. in Currie (1989), pp. 29-30; a second rendering of the same reported utterance gives: We have handed over Pithora alive to the army of Islam
suggested_refs: The Ajmer miracle cycle of the Siyar al-Aqtab; Currie's separation of the historical from the legendary Mu'in al-Din
sources: P. M. Currie (1989), quoted at second hand

stops.name: Ajmer, the marriage of 590
stops.date_confidence: devotional chronology only, 590 AH. It contradicts the Wikipedia and Currie account, which dates a marriage to the daughter of Saiyad Wajiuddin to 1209 or 1210. The two traditions are never reconciled by anyone who repeats either.
stops.campa: He marries Bibi Ummat-ullah. Three children are named in the devotional chronology: Fakhruddin, Husamuddin, and a daughter, Bibi Hafiza Jamal. The Currie-derived account gives a different marriage in a different decade, to the daughter of Saiyad Wajiuddin in 1209, and neither tradition acknowledges the other. The man who sold a mill to walk out of Sistan with nothing is now a householder in Rajasthan with a wife, children, a kitchen, and a queue of people at the door of it.
suggested_refs: The two incompatible marriage chronologies of the Ajmer years

stops.name: Balkh, the road back toward Baghdad
stops.date_confidence: internally inconsistent in its own source. Sufiwiki's chronology records a departure from Ajmer toward Baghdad by way of Balkh in 598 AH, 1200, while the same chronology holds that he has been permanently settled at Ajmer since 1192, and it duplicates the earlier Balkh recruitment of Maulana Ziauddin.
stops.campa: One chronology has him leave Ajmer and go back west by way of Balkh, taking Maulana Ziauddin as a disciple a second time, on a road toward Baghdad. The same chronology has him permanently settled at Ajmer since 1192. Both statements sit in the same document, and nobody who copies it out has noticed. This is what the record of his middle life is made of: a devotional calendar that counts first, third and fourth arrivals in Ajmer while sending him four thousand miles and back between them.
suggested_refs: The internal contradictions of the sufiwiki Chishti chronology

stops.name: Ajmer, the returns of 602 and 610
stops.date_confidence: devotional chronology. A third arrival at Ajmer in 602 AH, 1206, and a fourth in 610 AH, 1213, are listed as separate events, which means the tradition itself does not hold that he sat still. This stop carries both.
stops.campa: The chronology lists a third arrival in Ajmer in 602 and a fourth in 610, which means the tradition itself does not believe he stayed put. Between them the Delhi Sultanate hardens into a state: Iltutmish takes the throne in 1211, and the Ghurid conquest acquires a capital, a coinage and a court. The hospice at Ajmer is by now a fixed institution in a country rearranged around it, and the man inside it holds no office in the new order and takes nothing from it.
suggested_refs: The reign of Iltutmish, 1211-1236, and the consolidation of the Delhi Sultanate

stops.name: Ajmer, the marriage recorded by Currie
stops.date_confidence: attested as far as anything here is attested: Wikipedia, citing Currie's study of the Ajmer shrine tradition, gives 1209 or 1210. Even this sits inside a shrine tradition rather than a document. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: He marries the daughter of Saiyad Wajiuddin. This is the one domestic fact in the whole life that a modern historian will put a year to, and even Currie holds it inside a shrine tradition rather than a document. Three sons are counted across the sources, Abu Sa'id, Fakhr al-Din and Husam al-Din, and one daughter, Bibi Jamal. Fakhr al-Din will keep the teaching at Ajmer after him and die in 1255, which makes this household the first Chishti institution in India.
suggested_refs: Currie's chronology of the Ajmer marriages and the children of Mu'in al-Din

stops.name: Delhi, the khirqa to Baba Farid
stops.date_confidence: devotional chronology, 611 AH. The visit falls inside Iltutmish's reign, which is the one point where the devotional and encyclopedic calendars agree. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: He goes up to Delhi, stays at the khanqah of Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki in Mehrauli, and there puts the khirqa, the robe of investiture, on Fariduddin Ganjshakar. Baba Farid will carry the order into the Punjab; after him Nizam ad-Din Auliya will hold Delhi, and after him Amir Khusrow will put the order's language into Hindavi verse. The whole Chishti line of South Asia passes through one afternoon and one garment, and the garment is the only document of it.
suggested_refs: The khanqah of Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki at Mehrauli; the khirqa of Baba Fariduddin Ganjshakar

stops.name: Delhi, the Qutb complex rising
stops.date_confidence: context rather than event. The same Delhi visit is set against the Qutb complex under construction; no source records him entering it. Canonical Delhi pin inherited from ibn_battuta.journey.json. Month arbitrary.
stops.campa: A mile from the khanqah the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque stands on the plinth of a demolished temple, its arches raised by masons who had never built an arch, and Iltutmish is extending the minaret his predecessor began. This is the new order in stone. A hundred and twenty years later Ibn Battuta will sit as qadi of this city and describe the same complex, in a Delhi where the order Moinuddin is planting has become the establishment and the Chishti shrines are the ones the sultans go to.
suggested_refs: The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and the Qutb Minar under Iltutmish

stops.name: Ajmer, the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: devotional chronology, 620 AH. The licensing vision is reported only in a seventeenth-century hagiography, four centuries after the fact. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: He marries a second time, to Bibi Asmat, and a son is born, Khwaja Ziauddin Abu Sa'id. The seventeenth-century hagiography explains the second marriage by a vision: the Prophet appears to him in the flesh one night, and the marriage follows from it. The explanation is doing work. A saint whose entire authority rests on having renounced property and comfort has taken a second wife, and the tradition issues him a licence for it four hundred years after he is dead.
stops.quote: Mu'in al-din had a second wife for the following reason: one night he saw the Holy Prophet in the flesh.
stops.quote_source: Allah Diya Chishti, Siyar al-Aqtab (1647), translated and quoted on Wikiquote citing Currie
suggested_refs: The Siyar al-Aqtab anecdote licensing the second marriage
sources: Wikiquote, citing Currie on Siyar al-Aqtab

stops.name: Ajmer, the chillah on Taragarh
stops.date_confidence: undated, within the Ajmer years; the year is a placeholder. Coordinate corrected: the pool's 26.4419, 74.6103 sits about 0.8 km west of the hill. Taragarh Fort is at 26 deg 26 min 32 sec N, 74 deg 37 min 06 sec E.
stops.campa: Above the town, on the hill the Chahamanas fortified and the Mughals will garrison, tradition marks a retreat where he goes to keep his watches alone. The chillah is forty days of fasting and prayer in isolation, the discipline he learned on the road with Harooni sixty years back and has practised in every country he has crossed since. Ajmer now holds two of his places: the hospice in the town where anyone may eat, and the cell on the rock where nobody may follow him.
stops.quote: Each time he finished reading the Quran, a voice came from the unseen world saying, O Muinuddin! your recitation has been accepted.
stops.quote_source: Allah Diya Chishti, Siyar al-Aqtab (1647), translated and quoted on Wikiquote citing Currie
suggested_refs: Taragarh hill above Ajmer and the chillah attributed to Mu'in al-Din

stops.name: Delhi, Mehrauli, the death of Bakhtiar Kaki
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia's successors list gives Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki's death as 1235, the year before Moinuddin's own. Month and day not carried here.
stops.campa: Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki dies at Mehrauli, a year before his master. He is the disciple who carried the order to the capital and held it there while Moinuddin stayed in Rajasthan, and his tomb becomes the second Chishti shrine of India and the anchor of the Delhi line. The succession is already arranged and already working: Kaki at Delhi, Hamid al-Din Sufi Nagauri at Nagaur, Fakhr al-Din at Ajmer, Baba Farid moving toward the Punjab with the robe on his shoulders.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Qutbuddin Bakhtiar Kaki at Mehrauli, Delhi

stops.name: Ajmer, the death on the sixth of Rajab
stops.date_confidence: contested by six years. The standard modern encyclopedic date is 15 March 1236, 6 Rajab 633 AH, at a traditionally cited age of 93. One devotional chronology gives 6 Rajab 627 AH, which converts correctly to 21 May 1230. Both traditions agree on the day of the Islamic month and on the town; only the Gregorian year and his age diverge.
stops.campa: He dies at Ajmer on the sixth of Rajab, at a reported age of ninety-three, and is buried where he taught. The devotional tradition dates the death to 627 AH, the twenty-first of May 1230; the encyclopedic tradition dates it to 633 AH, the fifteenth of March 1236. Both give the same day of the Islamic month and the same town, and the two stand six years apart. The Urs kept every Rajab is a celebration, because the order holds that on this day he is not lost but arrives.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed to a final discourse to his disciples; untraced in Anis al-Arwah, Siyar al-Auliya or Siyar al-Aqtab in any translation fetched. Tradition, not attested text
suggested_refs: The annual Urs of Rajab at Ajmer Sharif

stops.name: Ajmer, the sultan at the tomb
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia records Muhammad bin Tughluq visiting the shrine in 1332, within a century of the death. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: Within a century the grave is a destination. Muhammad bin Tughluq, sultan of Delhi, is recorded at it in 1332, and after him the visiting does not stop for seven hundred years. Nothing about the man is documented from his own century, and the building over him becomes one of the best documented structures in India: every dome, gate, cauldron and canopy attached to a donor, a date and a reason. The least verifiable life in this atlas lies under its most verifiable roof.
stops.quote: The other miracle is that before his arrival the whole of Hindustan was submerged by unbelief and idol-worship. Every haughty man in Hind pronounced himself to be Almighty God and considered himself as the partner of God. All the people of India used to prostrate themselves before stones, idols, trees, animals, cows and cow-dung... Because of his coming, the Sun of real believers, the helper of religion, Mu'in al-din, the darkness of unbelief in this land was illumined by the light of Islam.
stops.quote_source: Amir Khwurd, Siyaru'l-Auliya, trans. in Currie (1989), p. 30; the chronicler's praise-narrative about Mu'in al-Din, not the saint's own words
suggested_refs: The visit of Muhammad bin Tughluq to the Ajmer shrine, 1332

stops.name: Ajmer, the Buland Darwaza
stops.date_confidence: attested with an attribution correction. Wikipedia and the architectural sources credit Sultan Mahmud Khalji of Malwa, commonly dated 1455; the pool's Ghiyasuddin Khalji (r. 1469-1500) is a minority variant, not an equal alternative. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: Mahmud Khalji, sultan of Malwa, expands the complex and raises the great northern gateway, the Buland Darwaza, some eighty-five feet of it. A minority tradition credits his successor Ghiyasuddin instead. This is the door the Urs flag is hoisted over and the door the pilgrims come in by, and it is built by the sultan of a neighbouring kingdom for a man who took nothing from any court in his lifetime and left instructions that his hospice was to take nothing either.
suggested_refs: The Buland Darwaza of Ajmer Sharif, c.1455, Mahmud Khalji of Malwa

stops.name: Ajmer, the marble dome
stops.date_confidence: attested. The date is recorded in gold lettering on the northern wall of the shrine. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: A white marble dome goes up over the grave, its date set in gold letters on the northern wall. A century later Shah Jahan will add a marble Jami Masjid inside the complex, and Aurangzeb the Sandali Masjid after him. The tomb of a man who owned a mat is being finished in the material the Mughals keep for imperial building, and each emperor who adds to it is buying, in stone, a share of a sanctity that none of them can manufacture on their own account.
suggested_refs: The 1532 marble dome and its gold-lettered inscription; Shah Jahan's Jami Masjid, 1637

stops.name: Ajmer, Akbar's first visit
stops.date_confidence: attested, with the pool's date corrected. Akbar's first visit was 1562, not 1566: Bharmal met him at Sanganer on 20 January 1562 and the marriage followed on 6 February. The fourteen-visit total, the 1568 deg and the 1579 sanctum reconstruction are confirmed.
stops.campa: Akbar comes to the dargah for the first time in 1562, the year Raja Bharmal meets him at Sanganer and the year of his marriage to the Rajput princess remembered as Mariam-uz-Zamani. He will return at least fourteen times across the reign and rebuild the sanctum in 1579, and after Chittorgarh in 1568 he sends the great deg, a seven-metal cauldron over six metres across, which is still filled and cooked in for pilgrims. Jahangir sends the smaller one in 1614.
suggested_refs: The two degs of Ajmer Sharif: Akbar's, 1568, and Jahangir's, 1614

stops.name: Ajmer, the sixteen stages from Agra
stops.date_confidence: attested, with the pool's generalisation corrected. Only two of the fourteen visits are documented as made on foot: 1568, in fulfilment of a vow for an heir, and January 1570, covering about 370 km in sixteen stages. Day within January unknown.
stops.campa: In January 1570 the emperor walks. Three hundred and seventy kilometres from Agra to Ajmer, covered in sixteen stages on foot, after an earlier barefoot journey in 1568 made in fulfilment of a vow for an heir. Most of the fourteen visits are not made this way. These two are. The Mughal state at its height sends its sovereign down a road on his own feet toward the grave of a Khorasani who came into this town with forty men and no permission from anybody to be standing in it.
suggested_refs: Akbar's barefoot pilgrimages to Ajmer, 1568 and January 1570

stops.name: Ajmer, the Nizam Gate
stops.date_confidence: attested for the gate, 1911. The hereditary khadims and the tradition of a Brahmin family supplying incense, sandalwood paste and ittar since the saint's own era are tradition, not record. Month and day unknown.
stops.campa: Mir Osman Ali Khan, Nizam of Hyderabad and the richest man of his age, gives the yellow gate that is now the shrine's main entrance. The hereditary khadims keep the tomb as their families have kept it for generations, and a Brahmin family is said to have supplied the sandalwood paste, the incense and the ittar since the saint's own century. Hundreds of thousands come for the Urs, some twenty thousand on an ordinary day, and in 2008 A. R. Rahman writes the song.
suggested_refs: The Nizam Gate, 1911; Khwaja Mere Khwaja, A. R. Rahman for Jodhaa Akbar, 2008

stops.name: Ajmer, the notice to the Archaeological Survey
stops.date_confidence: attested, full date.
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of November 2024 a civil court in Ajmer issues notice to the Archaeological Survey of India on a Hindu Sena petition claiming a Shiva temple stood where the dargah stands. The Dargah Committee rejects the claim as divisive. Eight hundred years after a Persian dervish camped above Ana Sagar without anybody's permission, the question of whose ground it is has been reopened in a courtroom, and the hagiographies that credit him with the conquest are among the exhibits.
suggested_refs: The November 2024 Ajmer civil court notice to the ASI, and the Dargah Committee's response
